passage: Modern navigation apps calculate the fastest route from point A to point B in fractions of a second, sparing drivers the stress of reading paper maps or guessing traffic patterns. While this algorithmic efficiency offers undeniable convenience, cognitive neuroscientists warn that habitual reliance on turn-by-turn GPS directions weakens spatial memory. When drivers passively follow voice commands without paying attention to landmarks or overall street layouts, activity in the hippocampus—a brain region essential for cognitive mapping and long-term memory—drops significantly. Over time, people lose their intuitive sense of direction and struggle to orient themselves whenever technology fails or cell signals disappear. Occasionally turning off GPS on familiar routes encourages active mental mapping, keeping the brain's internal navigation system sharp.
